back: Experimenting on a system to build confidence in its ability to withstand turbulent conditions in production.
A test checks a known expectation; an experiment probes an uncertainty and either raises confidence or finds an unknown weakness.
Hypothesis around steady state; vary real-world events; run in production; automate continuously; minimise blast radius.
How much of the system and its users an experiment can affect. Limit traffic share, scope (instance before zone) and duration.
An automatic rule that halts the experiment and removes the fault when a guard metric crosses a threshold (e.g. CloudWatch alarms in AWS FIS).

front: When NOT to run a chaos experiment?
back: When you already know it will fail, cannot observe or stop it, during an incident or freeze, or when nobody will act on findings.
Netflix tool that randomly terminates production instances during business hours so services are built to survive instance loss.
Chaos Monkey, AWS Fault Injection Service, Gremlin, Chaos Mesh and LitmusChaos (Kubernetes), Toxiproxy (TCP proxy).
When fault X happens, metric M stays within bounds B. Needs a user-value metric, an exact fault and a numeric tolerance.
Stream starts per second (SPS): strongly patterned, so deviations stand out, and directly tied to customer happiness.

front: Why not use CPU as the steady state?
back: It measures internals, not user outcomes; CPU can look fine while requests fail, or spike while users are served well.
Traffic changes minute to minute; comparing equal slices at the same time isolates the fault's real effect.
Success: a weakness found at 1% of traffic during working hours. Fix it, then rerun the same experiment.
A scheduled exercise where a team triggers a failure scenario and practises responding: tests people, paging, runbooks and comms as well as software.
Google SRE role-play: an experienced engineer walks a newer on-call through a past incident, revealing what dashboards show as they ask.
Facilitator (injects fault, keeps time), responders (handle it as a real incident), observers (record what happened and what confused people).
